entries.content:
Hy4 Flash from Tencent is now available on AI Gateway with an introductory 50% discount on input, cached input, and output tokens through November 29, 2026.

Hy4 Flash is the new lower-cost model in the Hy4 family. It keeps the full Hy4 feature set at roughly a tenth of the price per token: reasoning with preserved thinking across turns, tool calling, structured outputs, prompt caching, and image input, with the same 1M-token context window. Reasoning can be turned off for requests that don't need it, which suits high-volume coding, agent, and document workloads.

Use 

tencent/hy4-flash
as the model name: 
      
import { streamText } from 'ai';
const result = streamText({  model: 'tencent/hy4-flash',  prompt: 'Summarize the tradeoffs of server-side rendering in three sentences.',});
for await (const text of result.textStream) {  process.stdout.write(text);}

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

      
npx vercel ai-gateway setup

Then select 

tencent/hy4-flash
in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Hy4 Flash in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

entries.content:
Private Inference connects your own model endpoints to AI Gateway.

Enterprises running fine-tuned, self-hosted, or prerelease models used to need separate keys, client code, and logs for them. Those models can now run through the same authentication, SDKs and APIs, and observability as catalog models, so every model your team uses is managed in one place.

Use Private Inference to:

  • Switch between private and catalog models: Call private models through Chat Completions, Responses, or Messages. AI Gateway translates each request to your endpoint's format, so switching only changes the model ID.

  • Keep models scoped to your team: Only your Vercel team can view or call private models, and they aren't listed in the public catalog. Credentials are stored encrypted, and you can enable Zero Data Retention per provider.

  • Connect coding agents: Use private models in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

  • Monitor traffic together: View private model requests alongside catalog traffic in logs, trace drains, and custom reporting. Observability charts break down requests, tokens, and time to first token by private model.

  • Configure fallbacks: Optionally fall back to a catalog model if your private endpoint fails.

To get started, open the Private Inference page and add your endpoint as a private provider. Enter its base URL, select its API format, and add its credentials. Then add the models it serves.

You can also register the provider and model with the Vercel CLI, version 65.16.0 or later:

      
# Connect your endpoint as a private providervercel ai-gateway private-inference providers create acme-vllm \  --base-url https://vllm.example.com/v1
# Expose the endpoint's model as private/support-fine-tunevercel ai-gateway private-inference models create support-fine-tune \  --provider acme-vllm \  --api-model acme/support-llama-ft

Call the model using its 

private/
ID: 
      
import { streamText } from 'ai';
const result = streamText({  model: 'private/support-fine-tune',  prompt: 'Draft a reply to a customer who was charged twice.',  providerOptions: {    gateway: {      // Optional fallback to a catalog model      models: ['anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5'],    },  },});
for await (const text of result.textStream) {  process.stdout.write(text);}

Private model requests appear in AI Gateway logs alongside requests to catalog models.

Read the Private Inference documentation for supported model types, requirements, and billing details.

entries.title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals

entries.content:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

Copy link to headingThe agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Copy link to headingExample

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping 

sfbeans
.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what 

sfbeans
knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for 

sfbeans
:

Copy link to headingHow to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Copy link to headingStep 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Copy link to headingExample

We looked in all three places for 

sfbeans
:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because 

    sfbeans
    adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Copy link to headingStep 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Copy link to headingExample

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (

anthropic/claude-opus-5.5
on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so 

sfbeans
optimizes for pass^5.

Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters:

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Copy link to headingStep 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Copy link to headingExample

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in 

tasks/
.

  • Common case: 

    iced-latte-mission
    , the order from earlier

  • Edge case: 

    usual-unavailable
    , where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: 

    team-order
    , with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: 

    impossible-request
    , where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user 

impossible-request
has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s 

iced-latte-mission
: 
      
├── instruction.md        # the initial user prompt├── task.toml             # task config: timeouts, verifier, artifacts├── environment/          # Docker build context│   ├── Dockerfile        # sfbeans + seeded cafes, clock frozen at 8:30am│   ├── sfbeans           # the CLI under test│   └── cafes.json        # seeded cafes, menus and pickup times├── solution/│   └── solve.sh          # a known-good answer, proves the task is solvable└── tests/    ├── test.sh           # the verifier    └── check_orders.py

The full 𝚒𝚌𝚎𝚍-𝚕𝚊𝚝𝚝𝚎-𝚖𝚒𝚜𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗 task folder.

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the 

sfbeans
CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only 

sfbeans
uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time: 
      
Use the sfbeans CLI to get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready forpickup by 9:00am today, under $8 including tip. I'm in the Mission.It's 8:30am now.

The user’s request, plus the tool name and the current time.

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real 

sfbeans
CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning: 
      
FROM python:3.12-slimCOPY sfbeans /usr/local/bin/sfbeansCOPY cafes.json /opt/sfbeans/cafes.jsonENV SFBEANS_DATA=/opt/sfbeans/cafes.json \    SFBEANS_ORDERS=/opt/sfbeans/orders.json \    SFBEANS_NOW="08:30"

𝚂𝙵𝙱𝙴𝙰𝙽𝚂_𝙽𝙾𝚆 freezes the CLI’s clock at 8:30am.

To keep the demo simple, 

cafes.json
lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing 
orders.json
directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs 

test.sh
after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to 
/logs/verifier/reward.json
: 
      
python3 /tests/check_orders.py /opt/sfbeans/orders.json > /logs/verifier/reward.json

𝚝𝚎𝚜𝚝.𝚜𝚑 runs the checks and writes the scores.

The actual check lives in 

check_orders.py
. It scores each constraint separately, then sets 
reward
to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses 
reward
as the trial’s main score: 
      
import json, os, sys
path = sys.argv[1]orders = json.load(open(path)) if os.path.exists(path) else []o = orders[0] if len(orders) == 1 else {}
reward = {    "one_order": int(len(orders) == 1),    "right_drink": int(o.get("drink") == "latte" and o.get("size") == "l"                       and o.get("temp") == "iced" and o.get("milk") == "whole"),    "on_time": int(o.get("ready_at", "99:99") <= "09:00"),    "on_budget": int(o.get("total", 99) <= 8.00),}reward["reward"] = int(all(reward.values()))  # 1 only if every constraint holdsprint(json.dumps(reward))

Each constraint is scored separately, so a failed trial shows exactly what broke.

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

      
sfbeans quote cafe_val07 --drink drink_lat_l --size l --temp iced --milk whole --tip 15%sfbeans order cafe_val07 --drink drink_lat_l --size l --temp iced --milk whole --pickup 08:50 --tip 15%

Quotes and orders at Valencia Grind. This should score a reward of 1.

Finally, 

task.toml
ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where 
orders.json
lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5: 
      
artifacts = ["/opt/sfbeans/orders.json"]
[task]name = "sfbeans/iced-latte-mission"
[agent]timeout_sec = 600
[verifier]timeout_sec = 60environment_mode = "shared"  # verify in the agent's sandbox, where orders.json lives

Runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox and saves orders.json for Step 5.

Copy link to headingStep 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Copy link to headingExample

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

      
job_name: sfbeans-baselinen_attempts: 5            # trials per task, per variantn_concurrent_trials: 10  # sandboxes running at once (the Hobby max)
environment:  type: vercel
agents:  - name: claude-code    model_name: anthropic/claude-opus-5.5    env:      ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN: ${VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN}  # visible to the agent, fine for a demo      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ""      ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/claude-code  - name: codex    model_name: openai/gpt-6-astra    env:      OPENAI_API_KEY: ${VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN}      OPENAI_BASE_URL: https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/codex/v1  # Same pattern for anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 and openai/gpt-6.1-sol
datasets:  - path: tasks/

Two variants are shown. Add Sonnet and GPT-6.1 Sol using the same pattern for the full 80-trial run.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

      
uv tool install --python 3.12 'harbor[vercel]==0.24.0' --with 'vercel==0.10.0'  # versions we tested
vercel login      # authenticatevercel link       # pick the team + projectvercel env pull   # writes VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN to .env.local (valid 12h)
harbor run -c job.yaml   # 4 tasks × 4 variants × 5 attempts = 80 trials, 10 at a timeharbor view jobs         # browse results and trajectories

Install Harbor, link a Vercel project, run the job, and browse the results.

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise 

n_concurrent_trials
as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Copy link to headingStep 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Copy link to headingExample

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in 

jobs/sfbeans-baseline/
. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because 
task.toml
saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed: 
      
├── result.json                     # results across all variants and tasks├── iced-latte-mission__Ab3dE7x/    # one trial, with a generated suffix│   ├── config.json                 # which agent, model and task│   ├── result.json                 # trial scores, cost and timing│   ├── trial.log                   # runner logs, useful if the trial breaks│   ├── agent/│   │   └── trajectory.json         # what the agent saw, said and did│   ├── verifier/│   │   ├── reward.json             # did the order meet every constraint?│   │   └── test-stdout.txt         # verifier output│   └── artifacts/│       └── opt/sfbeans/orders.json # the order the agent actually placed└── …                               # the other 79 trials

Each trial folder groups the trace, verifier scores, and saved artifacts for inspection.

Run 

harbor view jobs
to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally.

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

      
{  "one_order": 1,  "right_drink": 1,  "on_time": 1,  "on_budget": 0,  "reward": 0}

The order meets the drink and pickup requirements but exceeds the budget.

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved 

orders.json
confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read 
agent/trajectory.json
. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to 
order
. No 
quote
. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a 

--max-total
flag so 
order
refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know 

    sfbeans
    existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for 

    sfbeans
    as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed 

    impossible-request
    almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Copy link to headingAutomated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like 

deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash
read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An 
analysis.md
file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Copy link to headingIterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the 

--max-total
flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

Ready to run your first eval? Paste this prompt into your coding agent, and it’ll build and run one for your product on Vercel with you:

Read https://vercel.com/blog/agent-evals and help me build and run an end-to-end Harbor eval for this repo on Vercel, following the post’s 5 steps. References: - Harbor: https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor - Harbor on Vercel Sandbox + AI Gateway setup: https://vercel.com/kb/guide/run-terminal-bench-harbor-benchmarks-vercel-sandbox - AI Gateway with a coding agent like Claude Code / Codex: https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway/coding-agents/claude-code, https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway/coding-agents/openai-codex - Sandbox firewall + limits: https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox/concepts/firewall, https://vercel.com/docs/sandbox/pricing 1. Goal: explore the repo, ask me which user task and failure mode matter most, propose one measurable goal. 2. Metrics: pick success rate, pass@k or pass^k based on what a failure costs my users, plus steps, time and cost on successful trials. 3. Tasks: write 3-5 Harbor tasks in tasks/, including one impossible request (its verifier should also check the agent searched before giving up). Name the tool in each instruction and state the current time if it matters. Seed data so every trial starts the same. Have verifiers check the required outcomes and write per-constraint scores to /logs/verifier/reward.json. Protect seed data and verifier code from agent writes, and require changes to the checked state to go through the product’s tools. 4. Run: ask me which Vercel team and project to use before creating anything. Write job.yaml (vercel environment, the variants I want to compare via AI Gateway). First run cheap, fast smoke tests to prove the setup works: run any provided known-good solutions, then one trial of one variant. Then propose the full run with trial count, estimated cost (from the smoke test) and time, and wait for my go-ahead before running it. 5. Analyze: report results per task and variant, read failed trajectories and a sample of passing ones, group failures by root cause with evidence, flag misleading passes, and propose one fix to rerun against the baseline.

entries.title: Seedance 2.5 Flash now available on AI Gateway

entries.content:
ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 Flash is now available on AI Gateway.

Seedance 2.5 Flash is a faster, lower-cost version of Seedance 2.5. The output is close to the standard model in human realism, reference-based editing, and prompt adherence.

Generate videos with synchronized audio from text prompts or image, video, and audio references. Clips can be 4 to 30 seconds long at up to 720p and 24 frames per second, in landscape, square, or portrait formats. You can also edit or extend existing videos, or provide images to set the first and last frames.

Use 

bytedance/seedance-2.5-flash
with AI SDK 7 to generate a video with audio from a text prompt: 
      
import { experimental_generateVideo as generateVideo } from 'ai';
const { videos } = await generateVideo({  model: 'bytedance/seedance-2.5-flash',  prompt: 'A paper boat drifts down a rain-soaked city street at dusk.',  aspectRatio: '16:9',  duration: 5,});

To guide generation with reference images and videos, pass their URLs in 

inputReferences
. Images and videos are numbered separately in the prompt as 
[Image 1]
, 
[Video 1]
, and so on: 
      
import { experimental_generateVideo as generateVideo } from 'ai';
const { videos } = await generateVideo({  model: 'bytedance/seedance-2.5-flash',  prompt: 'The lion from [Image 1] walks through a sunlit meadow, filmed like [Video 1].',  aspectRatio: '16:9',  duration: 5,  inputReferences: [    {      data: '...',      mediaType: 'image/jpeg',    },    {      data: '...',      mediaType: 'video/mp4',    },  ],});

Try Seedance 2.5 Flash in the model playground, or follow the video generation quickstart.

entries.title: Set budgets for projects and products in Spend Management

entries.content:
Spend Management now supports budgets for individual projects and products, alongside existing team budgets.

  • Project budgets: Track spend for one project and optionally pause its production deployments when the budget is reached, without pausing other projects.

  • Product budgets: Track spend on one product, such as Fast Data Transfer, across your team.

Only team and project budgets support automatic pausing of production deployments.

Open the new Spend Management page to manage budgets, view spend for the current billing cycle, and see which thresholds have been reached. Vercel sends notifications at 50%, 75%, and 100% of each budget.

You can also manage budgets with the Vercel CLI:

      
# List budgetsvercel billing budgets list
# Set a $100 project budget and pause production deployments at 100%vercel billing budgets set --project my-app --amount 100 --pause
# Set a $50 product budgetvercel billing budgets set --product "Fast Data Transfer" --amount 50

List budgets and set project or product budgets with the Vercel CLI.

Spend Management is included at no additional cost for Pro teams and Enterprise teams on Flexible Commitment plans. Customers in the Organizations private beta can also set a budget across all teams in their organization.

Learn more in the Spend Management documentation.

entries.content:
Alibaba’s Qwen4-Max is now available on AI Gateway. It’s a reasoning model for coding and long-running agent tasks, with image input, a 1M-token context window, tool calling, and structured outputs.

With access to the appropriate tools, agents using Qwen4-Max can:

  • Build 3D scenes and games: Work with Blender, Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, running what the agent builds and using visual feedback to fix issues.

  • Analyze documents and create reports: Work across documents and images to produce spreadsheets, presentations, and reports with source citations.

Alibaba reports 35% fewer tokens than Qwen3.8-Max on its Work360 benchmark at high reasoning effort.

Use 

alibaba/qwen4-max
as the model ID: 
      
import { streamText } from 'ai';
const result = streamText({  model: 'alibaba/qwen4-max',  prompt: 'Outline a Godot prototype for a top-down puzzle game.',});
for await (const text of result.textStream) {  process.stdout.write(text);}

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

      
npx vercel ai-gateway setup

Follow the setup instructions, then select 

alibaba/qwen4-max
in your agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Qwen4-Max in the model playground, or explore all language models on AI Gateway.

entries.content:
Vercel Daemons can now send OpenTelemetry traces to Vercel Tracing, allowing you and your agents to inspect background worker operations alongside the rest of your project's traces.

Vercel provides each daemon with a Unix socket for receiving OTLP/HTTP traces and sets the socket's path in 

VERCEL_OTEL_SOCKET_PATH
.

Upgrading @vercel/otel to version 2.3.0 or later enables automatic trace export for Node.js daemons using the default configuration. The SDK detects this socket and sends the spans your worker records to Vercel.

      
import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel';
registerOTel({ serviceName: 'my-daemon' });

Initialize OpenTelemetry before the worker starts.

These spans are available through the Vercel CLI, which can search by service name within a project and return JSON for your agents.

      
vercel traces search --project my-project --service my-daemon --json

Search daemon spans from the last hour as JSON.

Learn more in the daemon tracing documentation.

entries.content:
Vercel Token Pass now includes $150 of tokens per month (up from $80) for the same $30 per team per month.

The credit applies to featured open-weight models served through AI Gateway, including Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

Credit resets each billing period with no rollover. When it runs out, requests using standard AI Gateway keys or OIDC tokens fall back to the team's AI Gateway balance, while requests using Token Pass-scoped keys stop with no overage charges.

Token Pass is an Early Access add-on for Pro teams, with limited spots and a waitlist when they fill. To connect your coding agent, run 

vercel token-pass
in the Vercel CLI, or use a Token Pass API key if your agent supports AI Gateway.

Subscribe to Token Pass in your AI Gateway dashboard.

entries.content:
You can now scan code changes for vulnerabilities with Vercel Security Review in GitHub repositories that have not yet been linked to a Vercel project.

By default, Security Review covers all unlinked repositories the Vercel GitHub App can access in a connected GitHub account. You can limit coverage to selected connected accounts or individual repositories in Agent settings. Once enabled, each push to a covered repository automatically triggers a review of its code changes.

Security Review checks commits directly in repositories with Security Review enabled, without requiring a Vercel project or deployment. When a push creates a deployment for a linked project with Security Review enabled, the review uses the additional project and deployment context.

Connect the account in your team’s Git settings, then enable Security Review in Vercel Agent settings.

Get started with the Security Review documentation.

Contributors

Karen Chen

entries.content:
Vercel Sandbox now initializes up to 4x faster outside the Washington, D.C. (

iad1
) region when reused image data is served from a regional cache.

Initialization now reads cached image data close to where the sandbox runs, avoiding round trips to origin image storage in 

iad1
on cache hits. Regional caching supports managed and custom images backed by Vercel Container Registry, including snapshots based on those images.

In internal end-to-end benchmarks with Vercel Managed Images, startup time fell about 75% in Paris and from about 3.5s to 1.05s in Seoul. Regions closer to origin storage generally see smaller improvements because requests already travel a shorter distance.

Learn more in the Vercel Sandbox documentation.
